# Figures

**52 PNGs, 300 dpi.** All are auto-generated by `python scripts/make_figures.py`,
whose defaults now cover **both** translation systems and all three protocols —
the bare command reproduces this whole directory. Inputs are
[`data/results/combined_long.csv`](../data/results/combined_long.csv) for the
back-translation figures, plus both backends'
`telephone_chain.csv` and `round_trip.csv`. Every plot here can be deleted and
recreated; they are committed for portfolio convenience but are not the source
of truth.

## Backend coverage at a glance

| Coverage | Count | How to spot it |
|---|---:|---|
| **Google Translate only** | 21 | filename ends `_google` |
| **NLLB-200 only** | 21 | filename ends `_nllb` |
| **Two-system comparison** | 10 | no backend suffix |

The unsuffixed files are the comparison figures. Note that
`chain_degradation_{cosine,bleu,ter}.png` and `asymmetry_heatmap.png` **were**
Google-only under an earlier version of `make_figures.py`; they are now genuine
two-system figures — one row per system and one column per system respectively.

---

## Per-family heatmaps — `heatmap_{translator}_{family}.png`

*16 files — 8 Google, 8 NLLB.* One per (translator × family). Each is a **2×2
panel of the four metrics** — cosine similarity (lexical), BLEU, TER, and
embedding similarity (semantic) — with **languages on the y-axis and domains on
the x-axis**, every cell annotated with its value. Useful for reading off any
specific (language, domain) cell.

Colour ranges are fixed across families and both backends (cosine 0.90–1.00,
BLEU 0–90, TER 0–100 with an over-arrow, embedding 0.60–1.00) so the same value
is the same colour in every panel. Bright always means better, which is why TER
uses a reversed map.

* `heatmap_google_{romance,germanic,uralic,slavic,semitic,east_asian,south_se_asian,turkic}.png`
* `heatmap_nllb_{romance,germanic,uralic,slavic,semitic,east_asian,south_se_asian,turkic}.png`

## Family bar charts — `bar_family_{metric}_{translator}.png`

*6 files — 3 Google, 3 NLLB.* Per-family bar chart with grouped bars by domain.
Error bars are ±1 SD across languages within the family.

* `bar_family_cosine_google.png`
* `bar_family_bleu_google.png`  ← *the figure to lead with*
* `bar_family_ter_google.png`
* `bar_family_cosine_nllb.png`
* `bar_family_bleu_nllb.png`
* `bar_family_ter_nllb.png`

## Domain bar charts — `bar_domain_{metric}.png`

*3 files — **two-system**.* One bar per domain, grouped by translator. Google is
solid and NLLB is hatched, so the comparison survives greyscale. This is the
clearest view of the domain-ordering reversal between the two systems.

* `bar_domain_cosine.png`
* `bar_domain_bleu.png`
* `bar_domain_ter.png`

## Cross-metric scatter plots — `scatter_{metric_a}_vs_{metric_b}.png`

*3 files — **two-system**.* Each point is one (language, domain) cell, coloured
by family. **One panel per translation system**, each with its own OLS fit and
its own Pearson *r*, *p* and *n* — the systems are not pooled into a single
cloud, because their correlations differ (0.651 Google vs 0.761 NLLB for
cosine ~ BLEU). The pooled value appears as an explicit footnote.

* `scatter_cosine_vs_bleu.png` — *the form-vs-meaning correlation*
* `scatter_cosine_vs_ter.png`
* `scatter_bleu_vs_ter.png` — near-perfect anti-correlation

## Box plots — `boxplot_{metric}_{translator}.png`

*6 files — 3 Google, 3 NLLB.* Per-family distributional spread across all
(language × domain) cells. Box shows IQR; notch shows median CI; whiskers extend
to 1.5 × IQR. Box fill uses the shared family palette, so a family is the same
colour here as in the scatter and radar figures.

* `boxplot_{cosine,bleu,ter}_google.png`
* `boxplot_{cosine,bleu,ter}_nllb.png`

## Radar charts — `radar_{translator}.png`

*2 files — 1 Google, 1 NLLB.* Three axes (cosine, BLEU normalised to 0–1,
1 − TER/100) and one polygon per family. Lets you see at a glance which families
are strong on form vs meaning.

* `radar_google.png`
* `radar_nllb.png`

## Correlation matrices — `corr_matrix_{translator}.png`

*2 files — 1 Google, 1 NLLB.* 3×3 Pearson correlation heatmap across
(cosine, BLEU, TER) for one translator, with significance stars. The diagonal is
masked, being 1.0 by construction.

* `corr_matrix_google.png`
* `corr_matrix_nllb.png`

## Telephone-chain plots — `chain_degradation_{metric}[_{translator}].png`

*9 files — 3 Google, 3 NLLB, 3 two-system.* Fidelity versus hop number, one
line per chain order (`linguistic`, `reverse`, `random`, distinguished by
linestyle and marker rather than colour). Columns are domains. Hop 0 is a
synthetic perfect baseline, so five hops are measured.

Per-system, one row of six domain panels:

* `chain_degradation_{cosine,bleu,ter}_google.png`
* `chain_degradation_{cosine,bleu,ter}_nllb.png`

Two-system comparison, one row per system with the system named in the row
label:

* `chain_degradation_cosine.png`
* `chain_degradation_bleu.png`
* `chain_degradation_ter.png`

Generated from both backends' `telephone_chain.csv`.

## Round-trip plots — `roundtrip_{translator}.png`

*2 files — 1 Google, 1 NLLB.* Per-language ABA vs BAB bars on each of the three
metrics, for the five round-trip languages (`ar`, `de`, `es`, `ja`, `ru`).
ABA is solid and BAB is hatched.

* `roundtrip_google.png`
* `roundtrip_nllb.png`

## Directional asymmetry — `asymmetry_heatmap[_{translator}].png`

*3 files — 1 Google, 1 NLLB, 1 two-system.* `|ABA cosine − BAB cosine|` per
language; rows are ordered by mean asymmetry across the systems present.

* `asymmetry_heatmap.png` — **two-system**, one column per system
* `asymmetry_heatmap_google.png`
* `asymmetry_heatmap_nllb.png`

Read the two-system version with the values, not just the colour: NLLB's
Japanese (0.504) and Arabic (0.293) are one to two orders of magnitude above
every other cell, so on a linear scale the Google column reads as flat black.
Google's spread there is 0.000–0.020, which is within noise, so no colour
transform was applied to manufacture contrast.

Generated from both backends' `round_trip.csv`.
